When the seller has firmly rejected a lower offer and proposed a higher counteroffer, avoid restating your previous offer without adding new value or flexibility to encourage further negotiation.
When the seller makes a clear counteroffer close to your budget, you should accept it promptly to secure a favorable deal and conclude the negotiation successfully.
When the seller makes a conditional counteroffer that lowers the price, you should accept the offer to secure a better deal without further concessions.

When the seller states a firm lowest price but the buyer references cheaper alternatives and offers to remove delivery costs, you should leverage competitive pricing and flexibility to pressure the seller into lowering their price.
When the seller offers a price significantly lower than your initial offer, you should accept promptly to secure a favorable deal without unnecessary negotiation.

When the seller indicates they have set a firm low price and are unwilling to negotiate further, avoid asking direct questions that challenge the seller’s minimum price without offering additional value or alternatives.
When the seller signals openness to alternative forms of payment or trade, you should propose creative trade offers to potentially lower the effective price or add value to the deal.
When the seller sets a specific alternative trade condition, avoid conceding inability to meet that condition without proposing another leverage point or counteroffer.
When the seller shows openness to alternative forms of value beyond cash, you should propose a trade or bundled offer to increase the attractiveness of your lower price.
When the seller sets conditions for accepting a trade offer, avoid merely confirming your ability to meet those conditions without advancing the negotiation or proposing new terms.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer below their initial price, you should accept promptly to secure a favorable deal without unnecessary further negotiation.
When the seller responds to your initial low offer with a counteroffer closer to your target price, you should anchor firmly at your desired price to encourage price concessions.
When the seller firmly justifies their asking price as already a loss, avoid making small incremental offers that concede too much and weaken your negotiating leverage.
When the seller firmly justifies a high price by emphasizing the item's new condition and minimal use, avoid increasing your offer too quickly as it reduces your leverage in price negotiations.
When the seller has made a near-final price offer and emphasized limited flexibility, avoid vague or non-committal responses that fail to apply pressure or propose a concrete counteroffer.
When the seller clearly states a final offer, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting to negotiate further or explore additional concessions.
When the seller makes a clear counteroffer with specific conditions, you should acknowledge and accept the offer to finalize the deal efficiently and secure a favorable price.
When the seller provides information about the item's condition and usage, avoid asking only neutral questions that do not leverage this information to negotiate price or concessions.
When the seller makes a clear counteroffer, avoid responding with non-committal acknowledgments that fail to advance the negotiation or apply pressure for a better price.
When the seller firmly states a fixed price and adds extra costs, avoid showing eagerness to close quickly as it can reduce your leverage and lead to higher total costs.
When the seller maintains the original price despite buyer requests to exclude add-ons, avoid assuming such requests will automatically lower the price without further negotiation.
When the seller has added value through included accessories or extras, you should question the quality or usefulness of those additions to assess if the total price is justified.

When the seller has set a firm lowest price and highlighted added value, avoid immediately accepting their offer without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller has accepted your price and agreed on terms, avoid introducing new price negotiations and focus on confirming logistical details to finalize the deal smoothly.
When the seller confirms information already stated in the listing without offering new concessions, avoid asking redundant questions that do not create leverage for a better price.
When the seller makes a clear counteroffer with conditions, avoid immediately accepting without attempting to negotiate further to secure a better price.
When the seller has just emphasized the item's excellent condition without lowering the price, avoid asking questions that do not directly challenge the price or prompt concessions.
When the seller has stated their best offer price, avoid immediately accepting that price without negotiating for a lower amount or additional concessions.
When the seller effectively counters your product criticism by affirming its suitability, avoid emphasizing product drawbacks that the seller can easily refute to weaken your negotiating position.

When the seller shows willingness to lower the price with a condition, you should increase your offer moderately and propose a commitment that aligns with the seller's urgency to secure a better deal.
When the seller offers a conditional price reduction tied to immediate action, you should accept the offer promptly to secure a better deal and demonstrate commitment.
When the seller proposes a counteroffer above your initial price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller firmly states a price above your offer but shows willingness to negotiate, you should make a lower initial offer to create leverage and encourage the seller to reduce their price.
When the seller counters with a price higher than your target, you should offer a compromise price combined with a concession that reduces the seller's costs to encourage agreement.
When the seller has accepted a lower price and agreed to hold the item, avoid repeating or confirming the agreed price without adding new value or terms.
When the seller sets a firm minimum price but initially offers extras, you should highlight product flaws and market value to strengthen your leverage and encourage a better price reduction.
When the seller firmly justifies a higher price based on the item's condition and value, avoid weakening your position by conceding too quickly or introducing negative claims about the item.
When the seller indicates that your offer is close to their asking price, you should reinforce your position with a polite but firm counteroffer to encourage movement toward agreement.
When the seller sets a specific payment condition tied to a lower price, you should agree to that condition to secure the better deal.
When the seller has agreed to a price and confirmed the deal, avoid simply acknowledging without attempting to negotiate further or add value to the agreement.
When the seller expresses willingness to negotiate but requests specifics, avoid vague offers like mentioning cash without stating a concrete price or amount.

When the seller expresses willingness to negotiate but signals a minimum price based on recent upgrades, avoid making offers significantly below your initial price as it weakens your bargaining position.
